learning: Tests whether the monotonic trend (0.10 m hurt, 0.12 m best so far) continues at 0.14 m. Read s-bend completions, max_error peaks and slalom line_loss_events per track. If the score falls, the track optimum is near 0.12 m and sensing becomes the next lever.
notes: Iteration 1 layout with wheel_track changed alone from 0.12 to 0.14 m. Controller identical to iteration 1, so the race isolates the track effect.
rationale:
Evidence: iteration 1 (0.12 m track, score 482.7) is the best design. Its oval finished 20/20, its s-bend 5/20 and its slalom 0/20, and every failure was an off-track end with max_error of 0.060 to 0.064 m while rms_error stayed at 0.023 to 0.030 m. Iteration 3 changed only wheel_track to 0.10 m and fell to 357.3 (s-bend 1/20, oval 14/20). Iteration 2 also used 0.10 m and scored 411.7, though it changed other fields too. Across the three clean or near-clean points, a narrower track has moved the score down, so the trend suggests the opposite direction should help.

Decision: keep the iteration 1 layout (7 sensors at 0.02 m spacing, span +/-0.06 m, 16 mm footprints, y = 0.06 m, mass 0.6 kg, radius 0.03 m, body 0.16 x 0.12 m) and change only wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.14 m. For the controller, I keep kp at 1.6 and every other controller field as in iteration 1. I do not scale kp with track width, because iterations 2 and 3 scaled kp down for narrower tracks and still lost score, so scaling is not the cleaner test. Turn rate per unit of turn falls by about 0.86x on the wider track, which acts as a damping effect on bend overshoot.

Expected result (hypothesis, not measured): fewer off-track ends on the s-bend and slalom, max_error below 0.06 m on more runs, and a score at or above 482.7. Main risk: the wider track slows the sharpest slalom turn, so line-loss events may rise there.
